Part-to-whole and hierarchies

Source: vignettes/articles/composition.Rmd
composition.Rmd

Charts that split a whole into its parts, flat or nested.

Chart Use it when
pie_chart() You split a whole into a few parts
treemap_chart() You split a whole into many parts, optionally nested
waffle_chart() You show shares as a grid of 100 squares
sunburst_chart() You explore a hierarchy with several levels
mosaic_chart() You show how two categorical variables combine
rose_chart() You show a cyclical breakdown, such as months, Nightingale-style
parliament_chart() You show the seats of an assembly and build coalitions

pie_chart()

pie_chart() draws one slice per category, with its share written on the slice, or next to it with a leader line when the slice is too small. Rows with the same label are added up, and without value the rows are counted, so raw data can be passed directly:

pie_chart(mpg, label = "class", title = "Cars by class")

Hover a slice or a legend entry to pull the slice out and see its value, its share and its rank. Click a legend entry to hide a slice (the shares are then recomputed without it), and double-click it to keep only that slice. Clicking a slice pulls it out.

Set inner_radius to draw a donut chart: a number below 1 is a fraction of the radius, a larger number a radius in pixels. The centre shows the total, and the hovered slice’s share and value:

energy <- data.frame(
  source = c("Nuclear", "Hydro", "Wind", "Solar", "Gas", "Coal", "Other"),
  twh    = c(320, 58, 49, 23, 34, 3, 8)
)

pie_chart(
  energy,
  value       = "twh",
  label       = "source",
  inner_radius = 0.6,
  center_label = "TWh",
  title       = "Electricity generation by source"
)

Pies are hard to read with many slices. max_slices combines the smallest categories into an “Other” slice (its tooltip lists them). Without a legend, the labels show the category names. start_angle and end_angle draw part of a circle, such as a half donut:

pie_chart(
  mpg,
  label       = "manufacturer",
  max_slices   = 7,
  inner_radius = 0.55,
  start_angle  = -90,
  end_angle    = 90,
  legend      = FALSE,
  title       = "Cars by manufacturer"
)

labels chooses what is written ("label", "value", "percent"), label_position where, and pad_angle and corner_radius separate and round the slices. fill sets the colours (a named vector maps them to the labels) and color_category picks a D3 colour scheme:

pie_chart(
  energy,
  value         = "twh",
  label         = "source",
  labels        = c("label", "value"),
  label_position = "outside",
  legend        = FALSE,
  pad_angle      = 0.02,
  corner_radius  = 4,
  highlight     = "Wind",
  color_category = "Set2",
  value_suffix   = " TWh"
)

In Shiny, input$<id>_clicked returns the label of the clicked slice.

treemap_chart()

A treemap shows part-to-whole data as nested rectangles whose areas are proportional to a value. Ben Shneiderman invented the technique in the early 1990s. It became famous through SmartMoney’s “Map of the Market” and the New York Times’ graphics of the US federal budget. Use it when you have many parts (optionally grouped into categories) and want to see at a glance which ones dominate the total. When you supply a group column, tiles are coloured by group and each group gets a header showing its total. Hover over a tile to see its value and its share of the total.

budget <- data.frame(
  department = c("Hospitals", "Primary care", "Public health",
                 "Schools", "Universities", "Vocational training",
                 "Army", "Navy", "Air force",
                 "Roads", "Railways", "Airports",
                 "Pensions", "Unemployment", "Family benefits"),
  ministry   = c("Health", "Health", "Health",
                 "Education", "Education", "Education",
                 "Defence", "Defence", "Defence",
                 "Transport", "Transport", "Transport",
                 "Social security", "Social security", "Social security"),
  spending   = c(5200, 2100, 800,
                 3900, 1800, 600,
                 2300, 1400, 1700,
                 1500, 1100, 400,
                 7400, 1900, 1300)
)

treemap_chart(
  data        = budget,
  value       = "spending",
  label       = "department",
  group       = "ministry",
  value_format = "$,.0f",
  title       = "Where the money goes (millions)"
)

Labels are truncated or hidden automatically when a tile is too small to fit them, so the chart stays readable even with many rectangles. In the example below, most of the 142 countries are too small to label, but you can hover over any tile to identify it.

library(gapminder)

pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

treemap_chart(
  data        = pop_2007,
  value       = "pop",
  label       = "country",
  group       = "continent",
  value_format = ".3~s",
  padding     = 1,
  title       = "World population in 2007"
)

waffle_chart()

A waffle chart is a grid of squares, 10 x 10 by default, where each category fills a number of cells in proportion to its share of the whole. With 100 cells, each square reads as one percent, so “about a third” or “fewer than one in ten” is visible at a glance. Readers find this easier to judge than pie slices. Pew Research Center, FiveThirtyEight, The Economist and the Washington Post use the format often, and in R it was popularised by Bob Rudis’s waffle package. Use it when a handful of categories make up a single whole, such as survey responses, vote shares or budget splits. Cells are allocated with the largest-remainder method, so the counts always add up exactly to the number of cells. Hover over a cell or a legend entry to highlight that category.

survey <- data.frame(
  response = c("Strongly agree", "Agree", "Neutral",
               "Disagree", "Strongly disagree"),
  n = c(312, 405, 158, 87, 38)
)

waffle_chart(
  data     = survey,
  category = "response",
  value    = "n",
  colors   = c("#1a9641", "#a6d96a", "#bdbdbd", "#fdae61", "#d7191c"),
  title    = "Do you support the new policy?"
)

You can change the grid size with rows and cols, and the fill order with direction = "col". The example below shows each continent’s share of the world population in 2007 on a 10 x 20 grid, where each cell is half a percent:

library(gapminder)

pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]
pop_continent <- aggregate(pop ~ continent, data = pop_2007, FUN = sum)

waffle_chart(
  data      = pop_continent,
  category  = "continent",
  value     = "pop",
  direction = "col",
  rows      = 10,
  cols      = 20,
  title     = "World population by continent, 2007"
)

sunburst_chart()

sunburst_chart() draws hierarchical data as concentric rings. It is inspired by the signature sunburst chart of Apache ECharts and reimplemented in plain D3. Hover over a sector to highlight its branch, click it to zoom in, and click the centre to zoom back out.

library(gapminder)

pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

sunburst_chart(
  data        = pop_2007,
  levels      = c("continent", "country"),
  value       = "pop",
  value_format = ".3~s",
  root_label   = "World",
  title       = "World population in 2007"
)

Without a value column, sectors are sized by row counts:

sunburst_chart(
  data        = mpg,
  levels      = c("class", "manufacturer"),
  root_label   = "Cars",
  label_rotate = "tangential",
  title       = "Number of car models by class and manufacturer"
)

mosaic_chart()

mosaic_chart() draws a mosaic (Marimekko) chart, inspired by the mosaic example in the Vega-Lite gallery. Each column’s width is that category’s share of the total, and each column is split into segments that add up to 100%, so every cell’s area is proportional to its count. Hover over a cell to see its count, its column’s share and its share within the column.

titanic <- as.data.frame(Titanic)

mosaic_chart(
  data   = titanic,
  x      = "Class",
  fill   = "Survived",
  value  = "Freq",
  colors = c("#e45756", "#4c78a8"),
  x_title = "Share of passengers and crew",
  y_title = "Share within class",
  title  = "Who survived the Titanic?"
)

When value is omitted, rows are counted. Factor levels set the order of the columns and segments:

cars <- mtcars
cars$cyl  <- factor(cars$cyl,  levels = c(8, 6, 4), labels = c("8 cyl", "6 cyl", "4 cyl"))
cars$gear <- factor(cars$gear, levels = c(3, 4, 5), labels = c("3 gears", "4 gears", "5 gears"))

mosaic_chart(cars, x = "cyl", fill = "gear", label_type = "both",
             legend_title = "Gears", title = "Motor Trend cars: gears by cylinders")

rose_chart()

rose_chart() draws a Nightingale rose, also called a coxcomb or polar area chart. It is inspired by the polar-interval rose chart of AntV G2. Every category gets a wedge of the same angle, and the radius follows a square-root scale so that each wedge’s area stays proportional to its value. An optional group column stacks the wedges. The example below uses Florence Nightingale’s own monthly death counts from the Crimean War, 1854–55 (the same values as HistData::Nightingale).

mon <- c("Apr 1854", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov",
         "Dec", "Jan 1855", "Feb", "Mar")
crimea <- data.frame(
  month  = factor(rep(mon, times = 3), levels = mon),
  cause  = factor(rep(c("Preventable disease", "Wounds", "Other causes"), each = 12),
                  levels = c("Preventable disease", "Wounds", "Other causes")),
  deaths = c(1, 12, 11, 359, 828, 788, 503, 844, 1725, 2761, 2120, 1205,
             0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 81, 132, 287, 114, 83, 42, 32,
             5, 9, 6, 23, 30, 70, 128, 106, 131, 324, 361, 172)
)

rose_chart(
  data     = crimea,
  category = "month",
  value    = "deaths",
  group    = "cause",
  colors   = c("#7fa7c9", "#e0645c", "#4d4d4d"),
  title    = "Causes of death in the army in the East, 1854-55",
  height   = 560
)

Use sort to order the wedges by size:

rose_chart(
  data        = data.frame(state = rownames(USArrests)[1:12],
                           murder = USArrests$Murder[1:12]),
  category    = "state",
  value       = "murder",
  sort        = "desc",
  value_format = ".1f",
  title       = "Murder arrests per 100,000 residents (1973)"
)

parliament_chart()

parliament_chart() draws the seats of an assembly as a hemicycle, one dot per seat. The parties form wedges from left to right in the order of the data, which is usually their political orientation. A dashed line marks the majority, and the centre shows the total. Hover a seat or a legend entry to see the party’s seats, share, rank and distance from a majority.

# The data is a toy example and does not reflect the reality
vote_results_germany <- data.frame(
  political_party = c("SDP", "CDU", "Linke", "Grüne"),
  number_of_seats = c(200, 40, 30, 20)
)
parliament_chart(
  data = vote_results_germany,
  categorical_column = "political_party",
  numerical_column = "number_of_seats",
  title = "German Bundestag",
  subtitle = "Toy results"
)

The chart is also a coalition builder: click the parties to put them together. Their seats glide to the left of the hemicycle, so the coalition has a majority when it crosses the dashed line, and the gauge underneath counts its seats. coalition sets the parties of the coalition when the chart is first drawn, previous shows the gains and losses since the previous election, and fill gives the parties their own colours. In Shiny, the coalition arrives in input$<id>_coalition.

assembly <- data.frame(
  party = c("Left", "Greens", "Social Democrats", "Liberals",
            "Conservatives", "Nationalists"),
  seats = c(28, 41, 152, 63, 187, 79),
  seats_before = c(39, 30, 171, 48, 170, 92)
)
parliament_chart(
  assembly, "party", "seats",
  previous = "seats_before",
  fill = c("#c0392b", "#3ca951", "#ff725c", "#efb118", "#4269d0", "#6b4e9c"),
  coalition = c("Social Democrats", "Greens", "Liberals"),
  title = "Who can govern?",
  subtitle = "Click the parties to build a coalition"
)

arc bends the seats into a horseshoe (or a full ring at 360 degrees), seat_shape = "square" draws square seats and majority sets another threshold, such as a two-thirds majority.

parliament_chart(
  assembly, "party", "seats",
  arc = 280,
  inner_radius = 0.5,
  seat_shape = "square",
  majority = 2 / 3,
  sort = "descending",
  title = "A two-thirds majority"
)
